tldr: A low-cost, life-sized dual-arm humanoid built with 3D-printed parts and an aluminum frame integrates gesture recognition, object detection, and LLM-based voice interaction, achieving over 90% accuracy in both interaction and manipulation tasks.
hero_caption: Appearance and key components of the developed humanoid robot. With a lightweight design combining an aluminum frame and 3D-printed parts, it features 12 DOFs across both arms, 2 DOFs in the head, a 7-inch LCD facial display, and a stereo camera.
overview:
Humanoid robots capable of natural, cooperative actions in shared human spaces are drawing significant attention as next-generation interfaces. However, cutting-edge platforms like Unitree G1, Ameca, or Atlas are extremely expensive and largely black-box, making them inaccessible for regular university labs and educational settings to easily test AI algorithms. On the other hand, existing small open-source robots lack the payload, degrees of freedom (DOFs), and physical scale needed for serious human-robot interaction (HRI) validation.

To address this, the authors set out to build an affordable, open, life-sized humanoid where researchers can readily integrate and test AI modules. Standing roughly 150 cm tall and weighing just 15 kg, this adult-sized upper-body robot was built at low cost using 3D-printed parts, off-the-shelf servo motors, and aluminum frames. For computing, it carries a Jetson AGX Xavier, adopting a two-tier architecture that splits tasks between high-level processing and a custom-designed controller board for real-time motor control.

On the software side, gesture recognition via MediaPipe and an LSTM classifier, 3D object detection via YOLO and a ZED 2 depth camera, and natural language understanding via speech recognition and an LLM (Gemini API) are integrated under ROS. In real-world validation experiments, the robot performed expressive emotional reactions to gestures and executed pick-and-place operations based on voice commands. Results confirmed strong performance—96% gesture recognition, 92% speech recognition, an average manipulation positioning error of 1.83 cm, and an overall task success rate exceeding 90%—demonstrating its value as a practical testbed for HRI research.
contributions: Developed a low-cost, life-sized humanoid platform using 3D-printed parts and an aluminum frame, featuring a 12-DOF dual-arm system, a 2-DOF head, and a 7-inch LCD for emotional expression.

Established a hierarchical hardware and software architecture cleanly separating a dual-MCU custom controller board for low-latency motor control from an onboard Jetson AGX Xavier running ROS and AI inference.
Integrated three AI modules: gesture recognition (MediaPipe + LSTM), 3D object localization (YOLO + ZED 2), and spoken language understanding (speech recognition + structured LLM semantic parsing).

Demonstrated accurate real-time operations in two physical scenarios—gesture-based interaction and voice-command pick-and-place—achieving an average positioning error of approximately 1.83 cm and over 90% task success rate.

sections.heading: Bridging the Gap Between Costly Flagships and Underpowered Educational Bots
sections.summary: While humanoid development is progressing rapidly, commercial high-end systems remain costly and closed, whereas open-source educational options lack power and physical scale. To fill this gap, this paper introduces an affordable, life-sized humanoid prototype capable of integrating advanced multimodal AI.
sections.details:
For robots operating in human-centered environments, natural communication using voice, body language, and facial expressions is essential. Recent years have seen impressive leaps with humanoids like Unitree's G1 and R1, the expressive Ameca, and the highly agile Atlas. However, a major barrier remains: these high-end platforms are prohibitively expensive, proprietary black boxes, and difficult to repair or modify, making them ill-suited for rapid AI prototyping in academic labs.

On the other hand, open-source platforms for education and research—such as NimbRo-OP2X, ROBOTIS OP2/OP3, and Poppy—do exist. While they lower the barrier to entry, their payloads are tiny and their DOFs are limited, leaving them underpowered for realistic manipulation or natural human-robot interaction.

Furthermore, despite recent AI breakthroughs combining large language models (LLMs) for command parsing with precise pose estimation, much of this work remains confined to simulation or stops short of full-body physical interaction on actual robots.

To tackle this, the authors developed an affordable, reproducible, life-sized humanoid platform capable of real-time multimodal processing across speech, vision, and gesture. The goal of this paper is to demonstrate the full pipeline: from hardware design and AI software integration to real-world interaction and manipulation benchmarks.

sections.heading: A Design Philosophy Connecting Affordable Hardware to Smart AI Modules
sections.summary: Built from a lightweight aluminum frame and 3D-printed parts, the robot has 12 DOFs across its dual arms and 2 DOFs in the head. A Jetson AGX Xavier handles high-level AI tasks while a custom dual-MCU board manages real-time motor control, seamlessly coordinating object detection, gesture recognition, and LLM-driven voice comprehension.
sections.details:
The system architecture is cleanly organized into two layers: the mechanical/electronic base, and the AI perception and control layer.

### II-A Mechanical and Electronic Structure
The robot's skeleton is constructed from square aluminum tubing, with joints and brackets fabricated from 3D-printed components. The aluminum ensures strength and rigidity, while the printed parts allow rapid design iterations and low-cost replication. It stands approximately 150 cm tall and weighs only 15 kg. An adult-sized upper-body scale was chosen specifically so actions like handshakes, waving, and handing over objects take place at a natural height for humans.

Each arm features 6 revolute DOFs (12 DOFs total), with forward and inverse kinematics solved using standard Denavit-Hartenberg (D-H) parameters. Commercial serial servos are utilized strategically: high-torque DS5160 units at the high-load shoulders, FT5330M at the elbows, and compact TD-8120MG and MG996R servos for wrists and grippers. This keeps costs down while providing a payload capacity of up to roughly 600 g.

The head has 2 DOFs for pan and tilt, housing a 7-inch LCD that displays facial emotion animations, topped with a ZED 2 stereo camera for RGB and depth acquisition. Electronically, a custom $12\times 12$ cm PCB was designed to eliminate messy wiring. An Arduino Mega 2560 with ample I/O pins manages the 12 DOFs of the arms, while an Arduino Uno handles the head and auxiliary sensors, synchronized via I2C. An onboard NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier serves as the high-level brain, taking on computationally heavy tasks like vision processing and LLM inference over ROS.

### II-B AI Integration and Software Architecture
The software governing perception and interaction consists of three standalone modules:

### II-B 1 Object recognition
YOLO is applied to RGB frames from the ZED 2 camera to detect object bounding boxes. These 2D coordinates are back-projected into 3D world coordinates $(X_r, Y_r, Z_r)$ using the stereo depth map and checkerboard-calibrated intrinsic parameters. Solving inverse kinematics for these 3D points generates accurate picking motions.

### II-B 2 Gesture recognition
To capture nonverbal human cues, MediaPipe Pose extracts 2D skeletal keypoints in real time, feeding their temporal sequences into an LSTM classifier to recognize actions like waving, handshakes, and a heart ("Love") gesture. Depending on the recognition result, the robot returns responsive gestures, such as waving back or showing a smiling face on the LCD.

### II-B 3 Voice Command Understanding
Spoken input picked up by a directional microphone is transcribed into text using the SpeechRecognition library and fed into an LLM via a prompt. Crucially, the LLM is prompted to return a structured JSON output specifying action, target object, and destination. For instance, the utterance "pick up the cup and place it on the plate" yields a JSON with `action: [pick, place]`, `objects: cup`, and `destination: plate`. This output is merged with the 3D coordinates from the vision module to produce concrete manipulation commands.

sections.heading: Putting It to the Test: Gesture Interaction and Voice Pick-and-Place
sections.summary: With the robot mounted in a static standing setup, two scenarios were evaluated: gesture-based interaction and voice-command pick-and-place. The LSTM gesture classifier scored 96% accuracy, LLM semantic parsing reached 96%, vision-guided picking error averaged about 1.83 cm, and overall task success topped 90%.
sections.details:
To validate the practical utility of the proposed platform, quantitative evaluations were conducted across two scenarios in a controlled lab setting with minimized lighting variations.

### III-A Experimental setup
The robot was mounted upright on a fixed base, interacting with users via its head camera and directional microphone.

### III-A 1 Scenario 1: Gesture-based Interaction
The robot recognized gestures from a user standing about 1.5 m away. In response to waving, offering a handshake, or making a heart gesture, the robot answered with appropriate arm motions and animated facial expressions on the LCD.

### III-A 2 Scenario 2: Voice-command Execution and Object Detection
Natural language voice instructions such as "pick up the cup and place it on the plate" were given. YOLO localized target objects on the table in 3D, and the dual arms solved inverse kinematics to grasp, transport, and place them.

### III-B Results and Evaluation
Both individual AI modules and the integrated system demonstrated solid performance.

### III-B 1 Gesture Recognition Performance
The LSTM gesture recognition achieved 96% accuracy. The average latency from gesture completion to the start of the robot's motion was 1.2 seconds—a practical response time. As shown in Figure F5, when a user forms a heart gesture, the robot mimics the pose with its arms and displays a smile on its face screen, achieving natural interaction.

### III-B 2 Voice Command and Object Detection Accuracy
Across 300 voice command trials, speech recognition accuracy reached 92%, and LLM intent extraction accuracy reached 96%. YOLO maintained over 90% object detection accuracy. Although an external Gemini API was queried, instructing the model to output minimal JSON kept the token count low, capping the average response time at roughly 2 seconds. As shown in Figure F6, the robot successfully grasped the specified object and transferred it into a box as instructed.

### III-B 3 Positioning and Manipulation Precision
Measuring the end-effector positioning accuracy revealed an average error of about 1.3 cm against target coordinates in isolation. Even in the integrated setup—where YOLO detection and coordinate transformation noise were present—positioning error averaged just 1.83 cm. The overall pick-and-place task success rate reached roughly 90%, proving that despite using inexpensive servos and 3D-printed parts, the system delivers sufficient precision for practical use.

captions.F5: The robot recognizing a user's heart gesture and responding with a matching pose and facial expression. Real-time skeletal extraction with MediaPipe and LSTM classification perform with high accuracy.
captions.F6: Object recognition and pick-and-place execution based on voice commands. Real-time YOLO detection bounding boxes are displayed, and the right gripper securely grasps the target object and carries it to the goal location.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Next Steps: Moving Toward Local LLMs
sections.summary: The authors developed an affordable, extensible humanoid prototype, demonstrating high accuracy in multimodal interaction and manipulation spanning vision, gestures, and voice. Latency and connectivity limits from relying on an external LLM API remain current hurdles, pointing toward future adoption of on-device small language models.
sections.details:
This study presented and evaluated a humanoid robot as a practical, open testbed for HRI research, equipped with 12-DOF dual arms, an expressive 2-DOF head, a custom controller board, and a Jetson AGX Xavier.

With 96% gesture recognition via MediaPipe and LSTM, 92–96% voice command comprehension, under 1.9 cm manipulation error, and an integrated task success rate above 90%, the system demonstrated strong utility despite its accessible hardware build.

At the same time, the paper highlights a clear limitation: natural language parsing relies on a cloud-based external LLM API (Gemini). This requires an active internet connection and introduces latency jitter depending on network conditions. As a next step, the authors plan to adopt lightweight on-device language models (SLMs) running directly on the Jetson, aiming for fully offline, reliable, real-time responsiveness.

takeaways: You do not need an expensive flagship robot; combining 3D-printed parts, square aluminum tubing, and affordable serial servos is enough to build an adult-sized upper-body robot suited for HRI research.
Physically and electrically decoupling low-level servo PWM control (Arduino) from high-level AI inference (Jetson) significantly boosts system stability and modularity.
When using an LLM to parse robot instructions, prompting it for minimal structured JSON output keeps latency down to roughly 2 seconds, even with an external API.
Pairing YOLO with a stereo depth camera yields practical 3D localization accuracy, achieving an end-effector error of around 1.8 cm and a 90% pick-and-place success rate once properly calibrated.
limitations: The language understanding pipeline depends on an external LLM API, requiring constant internet access and leaving response times vulnerable to network latency.
The maximum arm payload is modest at around 600 g, preventing the handling of heavy objects or tasks involving strong external forces.
Experiments were limited to a controlled indoor lab with minimal lighting shifts and occlusions; robustness in noisy, crowded real-world environments remains unverified.
